lines.orig: Models can't read letters. They only eat numbers. So how does a word like Wednesday get in?
lines.visuals: The word 'wednesday' in big letters above a box labelled 'the model — only eats numbers', with an arrow and '[ ?, ?, ? ]' between them.

lines.orig: The simplest trick is one number per character. Our model starts with 35 base symbols. 26 letters, space, newline, six punctuation marks, and an unknown token.
lines.visuals: A grid of the 35 base tokens with their ids: <unk> (0), newline (1), space (2), a–z (3–28), and . , ? ! : ' (29–34).

lines.orig: But then Wednesday costs ten tokens, and the model has to re-spell every common word from scratch. Slow, and wasteful.
lines.visuals: ' wednesday' (with its leading space, shown as ␣) split into 10 single-character chips with ids 2, 25, 7, 6, 16, 7, 21, 6, 3, 27. Flash: '10 tokens for one word?!'

lines.orig: Byte-pair encoding fixes this. First, chop the training text into words, each keeping its leading space. Merges never cross from one word into the next.
lines.visuals: The corpus snippet 'tom has a blue boat. tom gives' is split into word pieces (tom · ␣has · ␣a · ␣blue · ␣boat · . · ␣tom · ␣gives), with yellow separators: merges never cross a word boundary.

lines.orig: Then count every pair of neighbors inside those words, across the first 400 thousand characters. The winner is space t, 13,558 times. Merge it into a brand new token, and repeat.
lines.visuals: Bars of the most frequent adjacent pairs inside words, in the first 400k characters of the corpus (the part BPE was trained on): '␣+t' 13,558, 'h+e' 11,868, '␣+a' 10,413, 't+h' 10,372. The winner becomes new token #35 '␣t'.

lines.orig: The first four merges already build 'the', with its space. Each merge is a rule, and the rules are kept in the order they were learned.
lines.visuals: Left: the first four merge rules (␣+t→␣t id 35, h+e→he id 36, ␣+a→␣a id 37, ␣t+he→␣the id 38). Right: '␣the' fusing from 4 characters into one token, id 38.

lines.orig: Do that 221 times, and you get 35 plus 221. A vocabulary of exactly 256 tokens.
lines.visuals: Big equation: 35 base symbols + 221 merges = 256 vocab size.

lines.orig: To encode new text, start from characters and replay the merges in the order they were learned. Space w goes first, then a y, then e d. Lowest rule number first, every time.
lines.visuals: ' wednesday' as 10 character chips; below, a panel shows the merge being applied. Merges fire in learned order: ␣+w → ␣w (rank 9), a+y → ay (rank 10), e+d → ed (rank 13).

lines.orig: Then e s. Then d plus ay makes day, and es plus day makes esday. Ten characters, four tokens.
lines.visuals: Remaining merges: e+s → es, d+ay → day, es+day → esday. Final result: ␣w (43) · ed (47) · n (16) · esday (202) — 4 tokens.

lines.orig: Notice the splits ignore grammar. 'esday' exists because Tuesday and Wednesday share it. Jumping becomes space, j, um, p, ing. The model never sees inside a token.
lines.visuals: Examples: ' tuesday' → ␣t · u · esday (shares 'esday', id 202, with wednesday); ' jumping' → ␣ · j · um · p · ing.

lines.orig: Frequent words get a token all to themselves. Space red is just ID 157, one single chunk.
One catch. This tiny world is all lowercase, so a capital W becomes the unknown token. Most real tokenizers start from the 256 possible bytes instead, so nothing is ever unknown.
lines.visuals: 'Wednesday' with a capital W encodes as <unk> (id 0) · ed · n · esday: TinyGPT's vocab is lowercase only. Note: most real tokenizers start from the 256 possible bytes, so nothing is ever unknown.

lines.orig: Our vocab has 256 entries. GPT-2 had 50,257. Newer models go past 100 thousand. Same algorithm, bigger table.
lines.visuals: Vocab-size bars to scale: TinyGPT 256 (a sliver), GPT-2 50,257, newer LLMs drawn at 100,000 with an arrow for 'and up'. Flash: 'same algorithm, bigger table'.

lines.orig: A bigger vocab means shorter sequences, but a bigger embedding table. It's a knob you'll get to turn when you build your own.
lines.visuals: Trade-off: bigger vocab → fewer tokens per sentence but a bigger embedding table (TinyGPT 256×64 = 16,384 numbers; GPT-2 50,257×768 = 38.6 million).
